title: They Wanted the Reputation of Surrender Without the Cost of Surrender
paragraphs: They Wanted the Reputation of Surrender Without the Cost of Surrender

Ananias and Sapphira looked like people who had placed everything at the feet of Jesus. The terrifying problem was not that they kept some of the money. It was that they wanted the church to believe they had surrendered what they had secretly decided to keep—and Acts 5 still asks every Christian a question we would rather avoid: What if the most dangerous place to hide from God is behind the appearance of devotion?
There is a kind of Christianity that can fool almost everyone.
It knows when to raise its hands.
It knows the vocabulary.
It knows how to say, “God has been so good.”
It knows what Scripture to post when life is falling apart.
It knows how to look surrendered without surrendering.
And that is what makes the story of Ananias and Sapphira so disturbing.
Because when we read Acts 5, our instinct is to keep them safely inside the category of “terrible people.”
Liars.
Hypocrites.
People who did something so outrageous that surely their story has very little to do with ours.
But Scripture will not let us escape that easily.
Their sin wore religious clothing.
Their deception happened in the middle of a spiritual awakening.
Their scandal did not begin in a pagan temple.
It happened among believers.
It happened around generosity.
It happened while people were talking about Jesus.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable detail of all is this:
From the outside, what they were doing looked remarkably like surrender.
That is why this story can get painfully personal.
Acts 4 describes an extraordinary moment in the early church. Believers were united. Needs were being met. Some who owned lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds to the apostles.
Then Luke gives us a specific example.
Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, sold a field and “brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet” (Acts 4:36–37).
Then the next words arrive:
“Ἀνὴρ δέ τις Ἁνανίας ὀνόματι…”
“But a certain man named Ananias…”
That little transition matters.
Luke has just shown us an act of genuine generosity, and immediately afterward he introduces Ananias and Sapphira.
Acts 5:1–2 tells us that Ananias sold a possession, with his wife’s knowledge, and kept back part of the proceeds while bringing only a portion and laying it at the apostles’ feet.
The Greek verb Luke uses is devastatingly interesting:
ἐνοσφίσατο — enosphisato
It carries the sense of secretly keeping back, appropriating, or withholding something.
The issue was not merely that Ananias possessed money.
And this is where careless readings of the passage can miss the point.
Peter explicitly says to Ananias:
“While it remained, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?” (Acts 5:4).
In other words, Peter does not accuse him of failing to donate one hundred percent.
The property was his.
The money was at his disposal.
Christian generosity in this passage was not a forced confiscation program.
Ananias was not struck down because God demanded every coin in his possession.
Something much darker was happening.
He apparently wanted to present one reality while secretly living another.
He wanted the act at the apostles’ feet to say something that his hidden decision did not.

And although Scripture does not give us a sentence saying, “Ananias wanted Barnabas’s reputation,” Luke’s deliberate placement of these accounts creates a sobering contrast between transparent generosity and deceptive generosity. We should not claim to know every hidden motive God has not revealed, but the text unmistakably exposes the attempt to create an appearance that was not true.
That is where the story stops being ancient.
Because you can surrender money without surrendering your heart.
You can surrender time without surrendering your pride.
You can surrender a ministry position without surrendering your hunger to be admired.
You can surrender publicly while negotiating privately.
You can tell everyone, “Jesus has all of me,” while quietly protecting the room in your soul where you have hung a sign saying:
Do not enter.
Maybe nobody knows about your room.
Maybe it is lust.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe an affair you keep calling “just talking.”
Maybe greed.
Maybe envy.
Maybe the addiction you delete from your history but refuse to drag into the light.
Maybe resentment toward someone you publicly say you have forgiven.
Maybe the desperate need to be noticed.
Maybe your Christianity has slowly become more concerned with appearing close to Jesus than actually being close to Jesus.
People see the worship.
God sees the war.
People see the Bible verse.
God sees what happened before you posted it.
People see generosity.
God sees motive.
People see the marriage photograph.
God hears the silence inside the house.
People hear, “I’m blessed.”
God hears what you whisper when nobody else is listening.
And suddenly Ananias does not feel so far away.
Peter confronts him:
“Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit…?” (Acts 5:3).
The Greek is even more arresting:
ψεύσασθαί σε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον
Pseusasthai se to Pneuma to Hagion.
“To lie to the Holy Spirit.”
Then Peter says:
οὐκ ἐψεύσω ἀνθρώποις ἀλλὰ τῷ θεῷ
Ouk epseusō anthrōpois alla tō Theō.
“You have not lied to men but to God” (Acts 5:4).
Notice where Peter locates the crisis.
The heart.
“Why has Satan filled your heart…?”
This was never merely accounting fraud.
This was spiritual deception.
Ananias may have been able to control what the apostles saw.
He could control what amount appeared before the congregation.
He could control the story other people heard.
But he could not control what God knew.
Neither can we.
That realization is terrifying only until you understand the Gospel.
Because the same God from whom you cannot hide is the God who already knows what you are hiding and still calls sinners to come into the light.
There is a difference between being exposed and being abandoned.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
There is a difference between the Holy Spirit revealing your sin so you can repent and the enemy whispering that your sin means you should run farther from Christ.
Jesus did not come for people who successfully manufactured a reputation of holiness.
He came for sinners.
Real ones.
Dirty ones.
Ashamed ones.
Compromised ones.
People whose private histories would destroy their carefully constructed public images.
The Gospel begins where pretending ends.
That is why this story should frighten the hypocrite in us without destroying the repentant sinner in us.
Ananias hears Peter’s words and falls down dead.
Later Sapphira arrives, unaware of what has happened.
Peter gives her an opportunity to tell the truth.
“Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.”
She confirms the deception.
“Yes, for so much.”
Then comes another chilling sentence:
“How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord?” (Acts 5:9).
The Greek expression includes:
πειράσαι τὸ πνεῦμα κυρίου
peirasai to Pneuma Kyriou—
“to test the Spirit of the Lord.”
They had constructed the lie together.
Think about that.
Two people who could have helped one another repent helped one another hide.
Two people who could have said, “We need to tell the truth,” reinforced the deception instead.
There are relationships that pull us toward confession.
And there are relationships that make hiding easier.
Sometimes love sounds like, “I will protect your secret.”
But sometimes real, Christ-centered love must say:
“We cannot keep doing this. We need to bring this into the light.”
Imagine how differently the story could have sounded if, before approaching Peter, one spouse had looked at the other and said:
“No.
We are not doing this.
If we are giving only part, then we will say we are giving part.
We will not pretend before God.”
One moment of honesty.
One refusal to maintain an image.
One decision to stop hiding.
Scripture does not tell us that alternate story, so we cannot pretend to know what God would have done. But Scripture repeatedly reveals the heart of God toward those who genuinely repent.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Not if we manufacture a cleaner reputation.
If we confess.
The Greek verb there is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō, carrying the idea of acknowledging or confessing.
No spin.
No spiritual public relations campaign.
No carefully edited version.
Truth before God.
That is one of the strangest freedoms Christianity offers:
You can finally stop auditioning.
The cross has already announced that you are a sinner.
And the resurrection has already announced that sin does not have to write your final chapter.
You do not need to impress Jesus into saving you.
You cannot.
You do not need to convince Him that you are less broken than you are.
He already knows.
Christ died “for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3).
Romans 5:8 says that “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after the reputation was repaired.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after the secret became respectable.
Not after we finally became worthy.
While we were sinners.
This is where scandal meets grace.
And grace does not mean God looks at deception and shrugs.
Grace is infinitely more costly than that.

At Calvary, Jesus Christ—the sinless Son of God—bore judgment for sinners. The One who had nothing to hide was stripped before the world. The One in whom there was no deceit was treated as though He carried ours. He died, was buried, and rose again, and now forgiveness is offered not to people who successfully hide their scandal but to people who turn from sin and trust Him.
That is repentance.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a change of mind that is inseparable in biblical proclamation from turning toward God.
Repentance is not saying, “I am sorry I got caught.”
It is not deleting evidence while protecting the appetite.
It is not crying during worship and returning willingly to the same secret agreement with darkness.
Biblical repentance comes into the light.
It agrees with God about sin.
It turns toward Christ.
And grace meets us there.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere between Ananias laying money at the apostles’ feet and Peter asking why Satan had filled his heart, this stopped being an article about two dead people in Acts.
It became about you.
There is something you have been trying to surrender without surrendering.
Something you want Jesus to forgive but not touch.
Something you want freedom from eventually—but not today.
Something you have learned to disguise so well that people closest to you would be shocked.
Do not misunderstand what comes next.
You are not being invited to perform a dramatic confession for strangers on the internet.
Some matters require wisdom, pastoral care, accountability, professional help, restitution, or private confession to people directly affected.
But you are being invited to stop lying to God.
He already knows.
The question is whether you will continue hiding from the One who sees you completely.
David understood something about this when he prayed:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart… and see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting” (Psalm 139:23–24).
That is a frightening prayer.
It is also a liberating one.
Search me.
Not my neighbor.
Not the Christian who annoys me.
Not the preacher whose hypocrisy I can identify from three hundred miles away.
Me.
Search me.
Because Christianity becomes dangerously hollow when we become experts at identifying everybody else’s Ananias while protecting our own.
What are you keeping back while presenting yourself as fully surrendered?
Your reputation?
Your sexuality?
Your finances?
Your bitterness?
Your ambition?
Your phone?
Your private messages?
Your secret habit?
Your refusal to forgive?
Your need for applause?
Your future?
Your children?
Your relationship?
Your plans?
Maybe the thing God is exposing is not something everyone else would consider spectacularly scandalous.
Maybe it is simply that you have been using Jesus as part of your life while resisting His rightful lordship over your life.
Jesus does not call us merely to admire Him.
He calls us to follow Him.
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).
That is costly.
But do not confuse costly discipleship with purchasing salvation.
You cannot buy grace with surrender.
Salvation is the gift of God through Christ, received by grace through faith, “not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And that truth matters enormously here.
Because it would be tragically ironic to read Acts 5—a chapter exposing religious appearance—and then manipulate people into performing religious actions so they can prove something to God.
You do not have to buy anything to prove your surrender.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
But when grace has truly taken hold of us, it does produce generosity, courage, witness, service, and a desire to help truth reach other people.
So if this article helped expose something you had been hiding, do not let the moment disappear when you close the screen.
Come back when the temptation to perform becomes stronger than the courage to be honest.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading—not because you want to expose them, but because you love them—send this to them.
Send it privately to the person who has been disappearing behind “I’m fine.”
Sometimes sharing the Gospel is not about building an audience.
Sometimes it is about refusing to keep life-giving truth to yourself.
Or, if Christ has already brought you out of a season of hiding, tell enough of your testimony to give another person hope without disclosing anything unsafe or inappropriate.
Someone reading the comments may need to know that repentance is not the end of a person’s story.
It can be the beginning of restoration.
Tell them the truth.
He calls sinners to repent.
He forgives those who come to Him.
He breaks chains.
He exposes darkness because He loves truth.
He does not rehabilitate our fake identities.
He gives us new life.
Because the lesson of Ananias and Sapphira is not, “Give God enough money or He will destroy you.”
It is far more searching than that.
Do not build your spiritual life around appearing surrendered.
Do not mistake Christian reputation for Christian character.
Do not become so skilled at convincing people that you forget you are standing before the God who sees the heart.
And when He exposes something, do not run farther into the darkness.
Run to Christ.
Bring the truth.
Bring the shame.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the pride.
Bring the greed.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the secret.
Bring the part you kept back.
Not because your confession can purchase mercy.
But because mercy has already opened the door.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
The answer to hypocrisy is not better acting.
It is repentance.
The answer to shame is not a better reputation.
It is grace.
The answer to hidden sin is not another layer of hiding.
It is the light of Christ.
Ananias and Sapphira remind us how terrifying it is to manufacture surrender before the God who knows the heart.
The Gospel reminds us how astonishing it is that the God who knows the heart still calls repentant sinners to Himself through His Son.
So stop auditioning.
Stop editing the testimony before God has finished writing it.
Stop trying to look like the person grace is calling you to become.
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Turn to Jesus.
And let Him begin where your pretending ends.
Because the secret you are terrified Jesus will uncover may become the very place where you finally discover how desperately you need His grace.
